beats.summary: Flat woodcut-style tableaux, salt-white on ink-black: a full sea, then the sea standing up and walking out between one wave and the next, leaving whale bones like combs on the floor. The only narration in the episode, a nursery verse in subtitles: 'One night the sea grew tired of the shore, / took up its blue and closed the door. / It took its roar, it took its rain, / and promised dark it would come again. / So keep the lamp, and keep it bright — / the sea remembers every night.' Each couplet gets one image; the final image is a tiny lit lamp on a cliff, held against a black horizon that seems to lean. Smash-cut from woodcut lamp to the real Saltwick Light at dusk — and to Espen, 12, mouthing the last couplet in a sing-song sneer while village kids chant it as a skipping rhyme below.

One held wide shot: the Dry Sea at dusk, an ocean of air under a bruised orange sky, salt dust smoking off the flats like spray that forgot how to fall. The title surfaces out of the salt haze the way the rhyme's woodcut waves receded — same motion, reversed. Wind and one low score note; no words.

beats.scene: The Floor of the Old Sea
beats.summary: Espen scavenges below the cliffs among stone kelp and a drowned freighter that was never on any chart; he chips blue saltglass into his jar, which pulses faintly — he taps it like a dead watch, pretty junk. On the freighter's hull, under barnacle scars, old paint spells a fragment of the rhyme: IT TOOK ITS ROAR — and Espen rolls his eyes at finding the nursery song even down here. He pockets a fresh shard as the horizon goes the color of a closing door; far off, Orla's small hand-bell rings him home, thin as a bird. Turn: the storm is coming early, and he runs the bone-field with the jar knocking his hip like a second heartbeat.

Inside Saltwick Light: the nightly lighting is a liturgy of hands — Orla's salt-stiff fingers counting matches into a tin (nine left), trimming the wick, wiping the great lens until their two reflections bend across it. She speaks the ritual line as she strikes: 'Keep the lamp, and keep it bright' — and Espen answers with a merchant's arithmetic he heard in town: oil costs, no ships, dead law for a dead sea. Orla doesn't argue; she presses one match into his palm and says only, 'Ask the sea.' Turn: as she descends, we see what Espen doesn't — her hand leaving a red smear on the stair rail, wiped away with her sleeve. Plants: the match tin, the spare match Orla always tucks behind the lens 'for the night the tin lies to you.'

The storm arrives like a held breath released: rain fists the glass, the lamp gutters, and Orla climbs to tend it, reciting the rhyme under her breath the way other people pray. Mid-couplet — 'it took its roar, it took its—' — the words stop; we hear the bell in her pocket strike the steps before we see her fallen, small as driftwood on the spiral stairs. Espen gets her to her cot; she grips his wrist with terrible strength and finishes the couplet at him like an order: 'and promised dark it would come again.' Turn: for the first time in a century of nights at Saltwick Light, the lamp is a boy's problem — and upstairs, the flame is already drowning.

A duel told entirely in close-ups: wet wick, cracked chimney glass, wind screaming through a seam in the lantern room, and the match tin — nine, then seven, then four — each failure a small funeral of smoke. Intercut, quick as blinks, single woodcut frames from the cold open flash on each blown match: the sea standing up; the door closing; the dark leaning in — the legend bleeding into the real. On the shelf, unnoticed behind him, the saltglass jar is no longer faint: it burns a deep whale-road blue, brighter with every match that dies. Turn: the last match in the tin snaps unstruck between his fingers, the lamp goes out — and the jar's blue light is suddenly the only light in the world.

beats.scene: SETPIECE — The Sea Remembers (Six Minutes of Dark)
beats.summary: Full dark, and the Dry Sea keeps its promise: darkness pours into the basin like a tide with no water in it — the stone kelp sways, salt dust lifts and hangs like silt, and the cold-open woodcuts return as living shots, couplet by couplet, the legend coming true in the same compositions. Out of the black rise the Undertow: whale-vast slow shadows with faint rows of fin-lights, swimming up the night toward the cliff, and one surfaces so close its passage fogs the lantern-room glass with breath that smells (Espen's face tells us) of a hundred drowned years. Guided by the jar's glow, Espen remembers Orla's hands, not her words — feels behind the great lens and finds the spare match, dry as a kept promise; he shields it inside the open jar, strikes it against the lens frame, and the wick catches on the sixth minute. The beam swings out and the darkness recoils from it like water from a shore — light is dry land — and a mile-long shadow banks away beneath the beam, one fin-light lingering on Espen like an eye taking his measure.

Espen keeps the light until the sky greys, sitting exactly where Orla sits, her coat over his knees, mouthing the rhyme without any sneer left in it — the same couplet from the cold open, now load-bearing. He sets the saltglass jar on the lamp shelf facing the strait: not junk anymore, an instrument — a tide gauge for the wrong sea. Below, Orla wakes, hears the lamp still turning above her, and closes her eyes; her hand uncurls, and we see she's been holding a tenth match all along. Turn: the boy who did the arithmetic against the lamp now refills the tin without being asked.

First light, salt flats pink as the inside of a shell — and we hear him before we see him: dozens of small bells, arrhythmic, like a tide chart set to music. The Bellfarer climbs out of the Dry Sea in a wide hat and a coat sewn with bells, licensed crosser of the floor of the world, and stops where the beam of Saltwick Light meets the ground, respectful as a man at a border. To Espen's jar he tips his hat; to Espen he recites a stanza of the rhyme the boy has never heard — a last verse: 'And where a light forgets its keep, / the old sea rises from its sleep.' Turn/hook: 'The tower across the strait forgot. Three weeks dark.' Then, looking at the boy and not the old woman's window: 'Someone has to walk over and remind it. How fast can you learn to carry a lamp?'

The tease, wordless but for one closing narration line: across the strait at dusk, the far lighthouse stands dark — and around its base, coiled like rope around a bollard, something vast and patient breathes, fin-lights dimmed to embers. Back at Saltwick Light, Espen's jar on the shelf glows toward the strait, steady as a compass needle. Final subtitle, the legend's cadence completing itself over black: 'The sea remembers every night. Now someone must remind the light.' End card in the woodcut style of the cold open: two lamps on one strait — one lit, one an empty circle.

setpiece: Beat 7 — 'The Sea Remembers (Six Minutes of Dark)': the full-dark flood, the Undertow rising in the cold open's own compositions, and the spare-match relight.
hook_ending: The Bellfarer arrives at dawn wearing a coat of bells, recites a final stanza of the Withdrawal rhyme that Espen has never heard ('And where a light forgets its keep, / the old sea rises from its sleep'), and delivers the news: the lighthouse across the strait has been dark for three weeks. His parting question — 'How fast can you learn to carry a lamp?' — lands on Espen, not Orla, and the tease shows something vast coiled around the dark far tower.
why_it_works: The interleaved legend gives the renderer exactly what it does best — repeated, high-contrast compositions — and gives the audience a second-viewing engine: every woodcut in the cold open is a shot list for the climax, so the setpiece lands as prophecy fulfilled rather than surprise. The rhyme carries almost all the episode's language, which keeps subtitle count low and lets silence, hands, and light do the acting; Espen's arc is measurable by how he says the same couplet three times (sneer, panic, prayer). Plant-and-payoff is mechanical and satisfying — the counted matches, the spare match behind the lens, the jar graduating from junk to instrument, the bells heard before the Bellfarer is seen — and the hook extends the legend itself: the last verse arrives with the last character, so the next episode is literally the next stanza.
risks: The rhyme must be genuinely good verse or the whole spine collapses into preciousness — it needs one more polish pass with the room. Repeating cold-open compositions at the climax risks feeling like a clip show if the timing is off; the living versions must be wider, slower, and wetter than the woodcuts. Beat 6 and 7 together are six minutes of one boy and one lamp — pacing depends heavily on score and SFX design the treatment can't guarantee. Orla's blood-smear and tenth match are subtle enough that a distracted viewer misses her illness entirely; may need one more legible signal.
